newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Caspian oil pipeline wants to move fast but can't.
newsitem.headline: Caspian oil pipeline wants to move fast but can't.

text.p: A multinational consortium with an ambitious project to build a pipeline to export Kazakh crude oil to world markets is trying to move faster but is unlikely to meet key deadlines, energy sources said on Wednesday.
The Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) has revised upward the amount of oil it initially plans to move once the first phase of the $1.2 billion link is built.
But it will not meet a key restructuring deadline on September 30 that would have kickstarted the project.

"We're now looking at a higher system, a higher capacity, and the risk allocation has changed," said Ed Smith, general director of Caspian Pipeline Consortium Ltd and a project executive at the Oman Oil Company, a CPC shareholder.
"There are a multitude of issues that need to be worked out that make it a challenge to finish restructuring September 30."

CPC groups original shareholders Kazakhstan, Oman and Russia, which have a combined 50 percent stake, with Chevron Corp, LUKoil, Mobil Corp, Rosneft, Oman Oil Company, British Gas Plc, Agip SpA of Italy, Munaigaz and Oryx Energy Co.

Another Western executive at CPC said the consortium was working to restructure ownership so that U.S. companies directly or indirectly have at least a 30 percent stake to take advantage of a U.S.-Russian tax treaty reducing tax burdens. Currently the U.S. firms have just under 30 percent.
CPC's project to send the oil through an as yet unbuilt pipeline around the Caspian Sea, across Russia and to the Black Sea, is a cauldron of complex financing and geo-political issues.

"If you look at the entire pipeline, it does force us to reconsider the entire contracting strategy," said the second CPC source, referring to calls by Chevron and Mobil to build the pipeline in one go instead of in stages.
"It's probably appropriate to look at rebidding the job."

The U.S.-Italian Willbros/Saipem joint venture won a contract in August 1995 to build the first phase of the pipeline, from the southern Russian town of Kropotkin to a new sea terminal north of Novorossiisk on the Black Sea.

Chevron and Mobil, with no way to export oil from their giant Tengizchevroil (TCO) project in Kazakhstan, are eager for the pipeline to be built, since problems in securing an export route have kept them from increasing output as planned.
CPC recently raised the amount of crude it hopes to transport in the initial stage to 28 million tonnes a year by the end of 1997 from 15 million tonnes.
The original, total final capacity of about 70 million tonnes a year has not changed.

"The roughest edge is the taxation and liability issue," said one source in CPC, referring to profits, local and value-added taxes. "Earlier, CPC had been considered tax exempt, but now it might have to pay taxes."
CPC planned to begin construction this year and complete the pipeline by 2000, but industry sources say that timeframe is unrealistic.
The 1,500-km (940-mile) pipeline may also carry oil from an $8 billion Azeri-led Caspian Sea project as well as Russian oil.
But hurdles abound.

"There are several key issues, one of which is the role of Transneft," said a Western energy executive whose company is a CPC member, referring to Russia's state-run oil pipeline monopoly that is not a CPC shareholder but will be involved.
He said CPC wanted Transneft to handle day-to-day operations, but not strategic matters.
"This is a very complex deal," said Smith. "We've got 10 multinational oil companies and three governments working on a pipeline that will cross two countries."
